description: Classes, objects, and inheritance — model real things in code.

screens.body:
In Python, almost everything is an object: strings, numbers, lists. An object is a bundle of data plus the actions that work on that data.

A class is the blueprint; an object is the thing built from it. One blueprint (class Dog) can produce many objects (Bingo, Rex, Miso) — each with its own data.

code.snippet:
name = "Roli"
print(name.upper())  # a string object doing a string action

screens.heading: Everything is an object
screens.keyPoint: Objects = data + actions; a class is the blueprint.

screens.body:
You define a class with the class keyword, then indent its methods (functions) inside. Class names use CapWords — each word capitalized, no underscores.

Methods look like normal functions, but they live inside the class and always take self as their first parameter. More on self next.
screens.heading: Defining a class
screens.keyPoint: class defines the blueprint; methods are its actions.

screens.body:
__init__ (pronounced "dunder init") is a special method that runs automatically when you create an object. Its job: set up the object's starting data.

Data stored on an object is called an attribute. self.name = name creates an attribute called name on the new object.
screens.heading: __init__: the constructor
screens.keyPoint: __init__ runs at creation and sets starting attributes.

screens.body:
self is how an object refers to itself. Inside a method, self.name means "this particular object's name" — Bingo's name, not Rex's.

Every method takes self first so Python knows which object called it. Forgetting self is one of the most common beginner errors — if a method misbehaves, check self first.
screens.heading: self: the object talking about itself
screens.keyPoint: self means "this object"; self.x stores data on it.

screens.body:
You create an object — called an instance — by calling the class like a function: Dog("Bingo"). Then you use the dot to reach its attributes and methods: d.name, d.bark().

Each instance is independent. Change Bingo's name and Rex is unaffected — they were built from the same blueprint but they're separate things.

options: Runs bark on the object d
check.question: d.bark() does what?

screens.heading: Creating and using objects
screens.keyPoint: Make one with ClassName(); use the dot for its data and actions.

screens.body:
Inheritance lets a new class borrow a blueprint: class Student(Person) means "Student is a kind of Person." The child gets everything the parent has — attributes, methods, __init__ — and can add its own.

It's code reuse at its best. Instead of rewriting name handling for Student, Teacher, and Staff, you write it once in Person.
screens.heading: Inheritance: borrow a blueprint
screens.keyPoint: class Child(Parent) reuses the parent's code and adds more.

screens.body:
When a child class defines its own __init__, the parent's version gets replaced. super() lets you call the parent's version anyway — no rewriting.

super().__init__(name) means "run Person's constructor for this object, then I'll add my extras." Use it whenever the child extends rather than replaces the parent's setup.

options: runs Person's constructor for this student
check.question: super().__init__(name)…

screens.heading: super(): call the parent's version
screens.keyPoint: super() lets the child reuse the parent's __init__.

screens.body: The official classes tutorial (docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html) is the definitive next step — it covers everything here plus method overriding, class variables, and multiple inheritance, all with clean examples.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The official docs are your best next stop.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
